Scaled quail (Callipepla squamata) emerge from eggs weighing approximately 7.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 7.5 grams] at hatching, a neonatal mass that reflects the modest yolk investment characteristic of precocial galliform chicks. This initial wet weight represents the chick's mass immediately following emergence from the calcareous shell, and field data indicate that hatchlings quickly begin exogenous feeding under parental guidance. The age at hatching is calibrated to incubation temperature, with eggs incubated at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] producing chicks after an average of 22 days [ab = 22 days], though the duration can range from 21 to 23 days depending on local thermal conditions within the nest. The neonates are downy chicks that exhibit immediate mobility, departing the nest scrape within hours of hatching. Their small body mass imposes high thermoregulatory costs, and brooding by the adult female is essential during the first week post-hatch to maintain body temperature.

Development proceeds rapidly in this species, and the time since birth at fledging is approximately 3 days [tx = approximately 3 days], an exceptionally brief nest-attendance period among North American galliforms. By the third day post-hatch, the precocial chicks are capable of sustained flight and begin foraging independently, though they continue to associate closely with the adult covey for predator detection and roost-site selection. This accelerated transition from hatchling to fledgling is an adaptation to the semi-arid shrublands and grasslands of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where prolonged nest dependence would increase vulnerability to terrestrial predators such as coyotes and snakes. The initial wet weight of the newly laid egg, recorded as 10.3 grams [Ww0 = 10.3 grams], provides the endogenous nutrients that sustain the embryo throughout its 22-day incubation period at 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. The yolks of Scaled quail eggs are notably lipid-rich, supporting the rapid development of the precocial hatchling.

Juvenile birds undergo a protracted growth trajectory, with puberty occurring at approximately 200 days after hatching [tp = approximately 200 days after hatching], a timing that ensures young birds complete skeletal and feather development before beginning to breed. This age at sexual maturation allows first-year birds to reach physiological readiness during their first spring, aligning with the breeding season of established adults. The ultimate wet weight of adult females typically stabilizes around 177 grams [Wwi = around 177 grams], a body mass that represents a near-doubling of the juvenile mass attained at the onset of gonadal maturation. Males, in contrast, attain a larger adult body mass of approximately 191 grams [Wwi = approximately 191 grams], a sexual size dimorphism that likely reflects intrasexual competition for breeding territories and access to mates. Both sexes exhibit seasonal fluctuations in body mass, with peak weights recorded in late autumn as birds accumulate lipid reserves for winter survival.

First reproduction in Scaled quail occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals breed for the first time during their second calendar year of life. This delay beyond puberty reflects the time required for territory establishment, pair-bond formation, and the acquisition of breeding experience. Females produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], with clutch sizes ranging from 9 to 16 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 9 to 16 eggs per clutch]. The eggs are laid in a ground scrape concealed beneath cactus or shrub cover, and incubation duties are performed exclusively by the female over the 22-day period at 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], though few individuals survive beyond their third or fourth year due to high predation pressure on adults during the breeding season.

Comparative life-history analyses place Scaled quail among the longer-lived North American quail species, with a maximum documented lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] in wild populations. This longevity is accompanied by a relatively low annual reproductive output of a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], a strategy typical of arid-adapted galliforms that invest heavily in each nesting attempt. The adult female reaches an asymptotic mass of 177 grams [Wwi = 177 grams], while the male attains a higher asymptotic mass of 191 grams [Wwi = 191 grams], a dimorphism that underscores the role of body size in male-male competition. The species' life-history syndrome, characterized by rapid fledging at 3 days after hatching [tx = 3 days after hatching], delayed puberty until 200 days after hatching [tp = 200 days after hatching], and first breeding at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], is consistent with an ecological strategy that balances high juvenile mortality against extended adult survival in a variable environment.
